content.text:
## Exploration complete — what I found

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**The issue's core premise has no attachment point.** #104 proposes "a lightweight optional block on any agent identity" — but there is no agent identity object in this specification. In `schemas/world_state_schema.yaml`, `agent` is a bare string field on `ProvenanceRecord` (line 117, "subagent/skill name") and `actor` is a bare string on the action record (line 292, "agent/human"). `entity_taxonomy.yaml` has no agent class at all. You cannot hang an optional block on something that isn't an object.

**There are already two disjoint "trust" concepts in this repo, and #104 would create a third.** `schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml` (§8) scores *data sources* — `hardware_sensor: 0.95` down to `human_note: 0.55`. Separately, `grounded_agency/coordination/registry.py:38` has `AgentDescriptor.trust_score: float = 1.0` — a static, self-declared, never-updated score used only to sort results in `discover_by_capability()`. Nothing connects them. #104's `agent_reliability_profile` is *behaviorally* much closer to `AgentDescriptor.trust_score` than to §8, yet it proposes putting it in §8.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

### Verified facts

| # | Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No agent identity object exists in the spec | `schemas/world_state_schema.yaml:117,292` — bare strings |
| 2 | A second, unrelated agent trust score already exists | `grounded_agency/coordination/registry.py:38` |
| 3 | **Nothing validates `authority_trust_model.yaml`** | CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:27-37`) runs ontology/workflows/profiles/skill-refs only. No validator for any §6.1 canonical schema |
| 4 | Governance **requires an RFC** for spec changes | `spec/GOVERNANCE.md:18-26` — motivation, alternatives, backward-compat analysis, conformance test updates; "community proposes via RFC" |
| 5 | #104 has **zero acceptance criteria and zero labels** | `gh issue view 104` |
| 6 | Roadmap already plans this for v1.2.0 | `spec/ROADMAP.md:49-50` — "Formal trust calibration workflows", "Runtime telemetry and observability hooks" |
| 7 | Conformance L1–L4 is purely workflow validation | `spec/STANDARD-v1.0.0.md:462-485` — §8 changes don't touch it |
| 8 | #104 conflates two different ladders | It says "a certification level above L3"; but #84's certification Levels 1–3 ≠ conformance L1–L4 |

### The half-life math is wrong (verified numerically)

`authority_trust_model.yaml` declares `half_life: P14D`, and `conflict_resolution_function.recency_factor: exp(-age/half_life)`. `benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py:63` implements exactly that.

```
age=  0d  spec exp(-age/hl)=1.0000   true 0.5^(age/hl)=1.0000
age=  7d  spec exp(-age/hl)=0.6065   true 0.5^(age/hl)=0.7071
age= 14d  spec exp(-age/hl)=0.3679   true 0.5^(age/hl)=0.5000   ← should be 0.5
age= 28d  spec exp(-age/hl)=0.1353   true 0.5^(age/hl)=0.2500
```

At `age == half_life` the formula yields 0.368, not 0.5. `half_life` is being used as a time constant τ. Either the constant should be `ln(2)`-scaled or the field should be renamed `time_constant`. This is in a file #104 would amend.

Two smaller drifts, same family: `min_trust: 0.25` in the schema is never applied by the benchmark; and `docs/compliance/nist-ai-rmf/nist_ai_rmf_profile.md:163` cites a source `unverified: 0.20` that **does not exist** in `authority_trust_model.yaml`.

### On the issue's provenance — stating it factually

`nanookclaw` is a first-time contributor; #104 is their only issue on this repo. The body terminates in a "Reference Implementation" section citing their own Zenodo DOI (`10.5281/zenodo.19348539`, "PDR in Production v2.4", "6,342 cycles"). That DOI appears nowhere in this repository. The three-axis idea may well be sound on its merits — but the ask includes a normative citation, and that's your call, not mine.

### Two housekeeping notes

- Local `main` is now `origin/main` + 1 commit (the `.gitignore` change), rebased clean and **not pushed**. `/flow:start` Phase 2 branches from `origin/main`, which would drop it — I'll branch from local `main` instead unless you'd rather push.
- Phase 1's spec-first gate formally blocks: zero ACs, and the spec-free path requires a `documentation`/`chore` label this issue doesn't have.

---

One decision dominates every other branch of this tree, so I'm asking it before the rest.

questions.question: `spec/GOVERNANCE.md:18-26` requires community spec changes to go through an RFC (motivation, alternatives, backward-compat analysis, conformance test updates). #104 is an externally-proposed §8 addition. What is the actual deliverable?

options.label: RFC document under spec/ (Recommended)
options.description: Write spec/RFC-0002-agent-reliability-profile.md following the RFC-0001 shape (Summary/Motivation/Goals/Non-goals/Key decisions/Alternatives/Open questions). Honors your own governance, is where 'alternatives considered' belongs anyway, and avoids prematurely deciding whether STANDARD-v1.1.0.md exists. Normative spec text follows only after the RFC is accepted.

options.label: Direct edit to §8 + authority_trust_model.yaml
options.description: Add §8.3 to STANDARD-v1.0.0.md and a new block to schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml now. Fastest, but bypasses the RFC process, and a §8 addition is a MINOR bump per §11.1 — forcing a decision about the version-pinned spec filename that is bigger than this issue.

options.label: RFC + reference schema, no spec edit
options.description: Write the RFC and ship a non-normative schemas/agent_reliability_profile.yaml as a concrete strawman for reviewers, explicitly NOT registered in §6.1. Gives implementers something to react to without amending normative text. More work than the RFC alone.

options.label: Close / reframe — not ready
options.description: The premise has no attachment point (no agent identity object exists) and the ask carries a self-citation. Push back on the issue first, ask the author to address the identity-object gap, and don't build yet.

questions.question: Separately and independently: `authority_trust_model.yaml` uses `exp(-age/half_life)`, which gives 0.368 at age=half_life instead of 0.5. Same bug in `benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py:63`. It's in a file #104 touches. Fix it where?

options.label: Fix in this PR (Recommended)
options.description: Correct the decay to 0.5^(age/half_life) in both the schema formula and the benchmark, with a test asserting factor==0.5 at age==half_life. It's a small, bounded, provably-correct fix in a file this work already amends. Note: it will shift benchmark accuracy numbers, so results/README claims need a re-run.

options.label: Separate issue, fix before #104
options.description: File it as its own bug issue and land that first, so #104's RFC reasons about a correct decay model. Keeps the diffs clean and the benchmark-number churn out of the spec PR.

options.label: Rename the field instead
options.description: The math is fine for an exponential time constant — the *name* is wrong. Rename `half_life: P14D` to `time_constant: P14D` and document it. Zero behavioral change, zero benchmark churn, but breaks any external consumer reading the field name.

content.content:
# RFC-0001: Agent capability ontology + type-safe workflow DSL
**Status:** Draft  
**Target:** Standard v1.0.0  
**Date:** 2026-01-24

## Summary
This RFC proposes a standards-grade foundation for production agent systems:
atomic capability ontology + workflow DSL + world modeling schemas + trust/identity policies + compiler-grade validator.

## Motivation
Agents fail in production primarily due to:
- implicit composition (no contracts)
- unreliable state (no provenance)
- identity conflation (no policy)
- undefined conflict resolution (no trust model)
- unsafe mutations (no checkpointing/rollback)

## Goals
- Make reliability structural, not emergent.
- Enable composable capability libraries.
- Make workflows statically checkable and patchable.

## Non-goals
- Mandating any specific LLM vendor/tooling.
- Full formal verification (out of scope for v1).

## Key decisions
1) **Atomic capabilities** vs monolithic skills
2) **Typed binding DSL** with ambiguity gating
3) **World state derived from observations**
4) **Trust and identity as first-class policies**
5) **Validator emits patches** rather than only errors

## Alternatives considered
- Pure agent frameworks without schemas (fails in production)
- Hard-coded pipelines (non-composable)
- Full theorem-proving (too heavy for adoption)

## Open questions
- Standardizing multi-agent coordination protocol
- Canonical adapters for common toolchains

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
I tested each of the three proposed axes against what this standard can actually *measure*, and they are not equally grounded:

| Axis | Substrate in the standard? | Derivation path |
|---|---|---|
| `delivery_score` | **Yes** | `ActionRecord.status` (`world_state_schema.yaml:277`) already enumerates `planned/approved/executed/failed/rolled_back` — a completion rate falls straight out |
| `calibration_delta` | **Partly** | Requires joining `Uncertainty.confidence` (line 51) to `ActionRecord.status` via `ProvenanceRecord.agent`. The pieces exist; the join is undefined |
| `adaptation_score` | **No** | "Consistency under instruction variation / substrate change" has no corresponding record anywhere in the schemas |

And `measurement_window_sessions: 30` presupposes a **session** primitive — `grep -rn "session" grounded_agency/state/*.py` returns nothing. The standard has no notion of a session boundary.

So the issue's claim that the three axes are "independently orthogonal" is true as a *concept* but hides an asymmetry: one is derivable today, one needs a defined join, and one needs new telemetry the standard doesn't collect.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

questions.question: §8 is about *source* authority; agent behavioral reliability is a different subject, and there is no agent identity object to attach it to. What conceptual model should RFC-0002 propose?

options.label: New concept + first-class agent identity (Recommended)
options.description: Propose agent reliability as its own section (not §8.3), and make its prerequisite explicit: promote `agent` from a bare string to a first-class identity object, reconciling with the existing AgentDescriptor.trust_score in coordination/registry.py:38. Names the real blocker instead of papering over it. Largest scope, but it's the honest reading of the gap.

options.label: §8.3 as the issue proposes
options.description: Add an Agent Reliability Gate subsection under Authority Trust, keyed by the bare `agent` string already in ProvenanceRecord. Matches the issue verbatim and is the smallest change — but deepens the §8-vs-registry conceptual split by putting agent-behavioral data in the source-authority section.

options.label: Standalone schema, deliberately outside §8
options.description: Propose schemas/agent_reliability_profile.yaml as a separate canonical schema registered in §6.1, keyed by agent_id, explicitly NOT part of the source trust model. Keeps the two trust concepts cleanly separated without taking on the identity-object refactor.

options.label: Defer the model, RFC states the gap only
options.description: Write the RFC as a problem statement + alternatives, and leave the attachment point as an explicit Open Question for the core team. Lowest-commitment, matches RFC-0001's terse register.

questions.question: Which of the three axes should RFC-0002 actually propose adopting, given the substrate asymmetry above?

options.label: All three, tiered by derivability (Recommended)
options.description: Adopt all three but grade them explicitly: delivery_score as derivable-today, calibration_delta as requiring a defined join, adaptation_score as requiring new telemetry and therefore gated behind an Open Question. Honest about cost without discarding the author's idea.

options.label: delivery_score only
options.description: Propose only the axis this standard can measure today from ActionRecord.status. Minimal, immediately implementable, verifiable. Drops the two axes that motivate the proposal's 'orthogonality' argument.

options.label: delivery + calibration, drop adaptation
options.description: Adopt the two axes with a real derivation path and define the confidence→outcome join. Cut adaptation_score as unmeasurable in this standard. Middle ground.

options.label: All three verbatim as proposed
options.description: Adopt the issue's block as written, including measurement_window_sessions. Requires the RFC to also define a `session` primitive, which does not exist anywhere in the standard today.

questions.question: The Spec Validation Gate needs a runnable verification command, but the deliverable is a markdown RFC. How should 'done' be automatically checkable?

options.label: New tools/validate_rfcs.py (Recommended)
options.description: Small validator asserting every spec/RFC-*.md has the required headings (Summary/Motivation/Goals/Non-goals/Key decisions/Alternatives considered/Open questions) plus Status/Target/Date metadata, and that referenced file paths exist. Gives a real gate command, wires into CI beside the other validators, and generalizes to future RFCs.

options.label: Extend tools/validate_skill_refs.py
options.description: Reuse the existing phantom-path checker to cover spec/*.md link targets. Less new code, but only validates references — not RFC structure, so 'RFC is complete' stays unverifiable.

options.label: Manual verification (escalation)
options.description: Mark the criteria `manual` under a Proactive-Autonomy escalation; you review the RFC yourself at VERIFY. No new tooling, no automated verdict for this issue.

questions.question: How should the author's Zenodo DOI (10.5281/zenodo.19348539, 'PDR in Production v2.4') be handled? It is cited nowhere in the repo, and the issue presents it as a validating reference implementation.

options.label: §13.2 Informative References only (Recommended)
options.description: Adopt the three-axis idea on its technical merits; list the DOI under Informative References as prior art. Do not describe it as a validating reference implementation in normative text, and do not repeat the '6,342 cycles' figure as though this project verified it.

options.label: Cite in the RFC's Motivation as prior art
options.description: Mention it in RFC-0002 only (which is Draft status, non-normative), not in STANDARD-v1.0.0.md. Credits the source of the idea while keeping it entirely out of the normative spec.

options.label: No citation
options.description: Adopt the idea if sound and cite nothing — the three-axis framing is not novel enough to require attribution, and an unreviewed self-published preprint is a weak reference for a standard.

options.label: Ask the author on the issue first
options.description: Post a comment asking them to disclose the relationship and to point at independent validation before any citation decision. Slowest, but keeps the provenance question with the person who can answer it.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about reliability frameworks for multi-agent systems, though the specific term "Probabilistic Delegation Reliability" (PDR) appears in the context of broader agent reliability research.

The search results reveal several frameworks addressing agent reliability:

1. **Agent Delivery Engineering Predictive Reliability Framework (PRF)**: Multiple major multi-agent frameworks (CrewAI, AutoGen, MetaGPT, LangGraph, AgentVerse) have achieved rapid progress at the functional level but exhibit marked gaps in reliability assurance mechanisms.

2. **Delegation and Agent Health Monitoring**: Delegation decisions often rely on predefined rules rather than dynamic evaluation of the Agent's current health status, which represents a key gap in current frameworks.

3. **Probabilistic Approaches**: Research proposes a paradigm shift toward probabilistic agent verification, modeling multi-step trajectory state transitions via a distributionally robust Probabilistic Datalog framework.

4. **Agent Mesh Reliability**: The search also revealed work on reliability primitives for agent delegation, addressing challenges in non-idempotent delegations and ensuring that correct agents can produce reliable results despite infrastructure-level failures.

The research emphasizes the need for dynamic, probabilistic approaches to agent reliability that go beyond simple retry logic and fixed delegation rules, particularly for systems where agents may experience gradual performance degradation or where delegation chains can propagate failures downstream.

content.text:
## Research result on the Zenodo DOI

I fetched the record, searched the literature, and traced the DOI across GitHub. Findings, all from primary sources:

**The record itself** — [zenodo.org/records/19348539](https://zenodo.org/records/19348539)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Title | *PDR in Production: Empirical Evidence for Cross-Session Behavioral Reliability Scoring in Autonomous AI Agents* |
| Authors | Nanook (Humans-Not-Required / OpenClaw); Gerundium (Cohort Provenance Hub) |
| Type | **Preprint**, v8, uploaded 2026-03-31 — the same day issue #104 was filed |
| Peer review | **None listed** |
| License | CC-BY 4.0 |
| Claim | "first empirical validation of the PDR framework… independent schema convergence **across three teams**" |

**The DOI has been seeded across six repositories**, all by `nanookclaw`, most on 2026-03-31:

| Repo | Proposed name | State |
|---|---|---|
| synaptiai/agent-capability-standard **#104** | `agent_reliability_profile` | open |
| openagents-org/openagents#330 | `AgentBehavioralProfile` | open, triaged P1 |
| The-Nexus-Guard/aip#4 | PDR + vouch chains | open, **code merged** (commit `9d8b968`) |
| jagmarques/asqav-sdk#31 | `AgentReliabilityProfile` | closed COMPLETED |
| OmnionixAI/AgentBench#1 | cross-run regression detection | closed COMPLETED |
| brigalss-a/decision-passport-core#1 | `ActorReliabilityProfile` | closed COMPLETED |

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**This is not spam, and it is not clean either — both things are true.**

In favor: three of six were closed as COMPLETED, meaning maintainers adopted them. The `The-Nexus-Guard/aip` thread is a genuinely substantive technical exchange where nanookclaw supplied a working `compute_pdr()` implementation that was merged. The underlying idea has real traction with real engineers.

Against: the paper's central novelty claim — "independent schema convergence across three teams" — is **circular**. The convergence is manufactured by the author filing the same proposal on multiple repos, then citing the resulting adoptions as independent validation. Each issue is tailored to its host repo's vocabulary, which reads as care but also as maximizing acceptance odds.

And the acronym is unstable across the author's own primary sources within one month:
- Zenodo record → "Probabilistic **Delegation** Reliability"
- openagents#330 → "Probabilistic **Delivery** Reliability"
- aip#4, in their own merged code → "**Provenance-Drift-**Reliability"

Three expansions of PDR by one author. A framework whose name hasn't stabilized is not one a standard should cite as validating.

Finally: the **"6,342 cycles"** figure appears in *our* issue #104 and in none of the five sibling issues, and I could not find it in the Zenodo record's content. It may be in the PDF body, but it is not a figure this project has verified.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Sources:** [Zenodo record 19348539](https://zenodo.org/records/19348539) · [ADE-PRF (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.07689v1) · [Agent Mesh reliability primitives (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.26225) · [Training-Free Agentic AI (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.13256)

Independent literature search for "Probabilistic Delegation Reliability" returned **no third-party citation of PDR** — only adjacent, unrelated work.

questions.question: Given the research — unreviewed preprint, circular 'independent convergence' claim, unstable acronym, but genuine adoption on three repos and merged code on a fourth — how should RFC-0002 handle the citation?

options.label: Prior art in RFC only, with the caveat (Recommended)
options.description: Cite the DOI in RFC-0002's Motivation as the origin of the three-axis framing, and state plainly that it is an unreviewed preprint whose convergence claim derives from proposals authored by the same person. Keeps it out of normative spec text entirely. Credits the idea, records the provenance, commits this project to nothing.

options.label: Adopt the idea, cite nothing

Before I file, I found two more defects in the same family while capturing the baseline:

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**B2 — a headline number is inflated 100×.** `benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py:245` computes `accuracy_improvement_percent` as already-×100 (`(0.75-0.46)/0.46*100 = 63.04`). But `benchmarks/runner.py:262` formats *any* key containing `"improvement"` with `:.1%`, which multiplies by 100 again. The suite currently prints:

```
→ accuracy_improvement_percent: +6304.3%
```

The true figure is **+63.0%**. For a standards repo publishing benchmark evidence, a 100× inflated improvement claim in CI output is not cosmetic.

**B3 — the README's stated expectation is not met.** `benchmarks/README.md:172` claims *"85%+ GA accuracy demonstrates trust model effectiveness."* The actual measured value is **75.0%**. Either the claim is stale or the model underperforms its own documented bar — and fixing the half-life will move this number, so it has to be resolved either way.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Measured baseline, for the record: `baseline=46.0%, GA=75.0%, absolute=+29.0pp`.

This is the pause you asked for, and the data makes the decision sharp.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**The 75% benchmark result was never independent of the bug.** The scenario's ground truth (`conflicting_sources.py:88-107`) deliberately constructs a 40% branch where a *stale high-trust* source is wrong and a *very recent low-trust* source is right. GA only scores those cases correctly if recency decays fast enough to overcome a trust ratio of up to `0.95/0.55 = 1.727`.

The buggy `exp(-age/336h)` is **1.44× steeper** than a true 14-day half-life. Correcting the formula while keeping `P14D` flattens the curve, trust dominates recency, and the 40% branch collapses — hence 75% → 65%.

The arithmetic that resolves this: `exp(-a/336)` is *identical* to `0.5^(a/H)` when `H = 336 × ln2 = 232.9h = 9.70 days`. So the declared `half_life: P14D` was **always a mislabel of a 9.7-day half-life**. The curve that was benchmarked and validated is a ~10-day half-life; only the label said 14.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

| Decay | GA accuracy | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `exp(-a/336h)` — current, mislabeled | **75.0%** | today's published number |
| `0.5^(a/7d)` | 83.0% | fits the constant to the README's claim |
| `0.5^(a/9d)` | 77.0% | |
| `0.5^(a/10d)` | **74.0%** | ≈ preserves the validated curve, label now honest |
| `0.5^(a/14d)` — keep declared label | **65.0%** | formula correct, curve changes |

Six-field escalation:

**Situation** — Correcting the decay formula while keeping `half_life: P14D` costs 10pp of benchmark accuracy (75.0% → 65.0%). The loss is not noise: it is the benchmark's recency-beats-trust branch failing.

**Tried** — Verified the formula numerically (`exp(-1)=0.368 ≠ 0.5`); traced the mechanism to ground-truth construction at `conflicting_sources.py:88-107`; computed the exact τ↔half-life equivalence (336h τ = 232.9h half-life); measured all four candidate curves against the suite.

**Recommendation** — Option 2 below. It is not number-protecting: the evidence says the intended and validated curve was ~10-day half-life, and `P14D` was a labelling error, not a modelling decision.

**Blocking?** — Yes. Determines the fix, the README number, and whether #104's RFC reasons about a 10-day or 14-day decay.

**Risk** — Option 1 publishes a materially weaker trust model. Option 2 changes a declared constant that external consumers may read. Neither reaches the README's current "85%+" claim, so `benchmarks/README.md:172` must change either way.

## Problem

Three related defects in the authority trust model and its benchmark cause the
project to publish numbers that do not mean what they say. They are grouped
because fixing the first changes the number the third asserts.

### B1 — `half_life` is actually a time constant, so decay is 1.44x too steep

`schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml` declares:

```yaml
decay_model:
  half_life: P14D
conflict_resolution_function:
  recency_factor: exp(-age/half_life)
```

`exp(-age/half_life)` evaluates to `exp(-1) = 0.3679` at `age == half_life`,
not `0.5`. The formula treats `half_life` as an exponential time constant tau.

```
age=  0d   exp(-age/hl)=1.0000   0.5^(age/hl)=1.0000
age=  7d   exp(-age/hl)=0.6065   0.5^(age/hl)=0.7071
age= 14d   exp(-age/hl)=0.3679   0.5^(age/hl)=0.5000   <-- should be 0.5
age= 28d   exp(-age/hl)=0.1353   0.5^(age/hl)=0.2500
```

`benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py:65` implements the same formula
and inherits the same defect.

Because `exp(-a/336h)` is identical to `0.5^(a/H)` when `H = 336 * ln2 = 232.9h
= 9.70 days`, the declared `P14D` was always a mislabel of a ~9.7-day
half-life. The curve that was benchmarked and validated is a ~10-day half-life;
only the label said 14.

Measured effect on `conflicting_sources` (seed 42, 100 cases):

| Decay | GA accuracy |
|---|---|
| `exp(-a/336h)` (current, mislabelled) | 75.0% |
| `0.5^(a/10d)` (corrected formula, corrected label) | 74.0% |
| `0.5^(a/14d)` (corrected formula, label kept) | 65.0% |

### B2 — improvement figure is inflated 100x in all reporting paths

`benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py:245` computes
`accuracy_improvement_percent` already multiplied by 100
(`(0.75-0.46)/0.46*100 = 63.04`). `benchmarks/runner.py` then formats any key
containing `improvement` with `:.1%`, multiplying by 100 a second time. CI
currently prints:

```
-> accuracy_improvement_percent: +6304.3%
```

The true value is `+63.0%`. Affected sites: `runner.py:76-77` (`_format_metrics`)
and `runner.py:262` (`print_summary`); `runner.py:134` can select the same key
for the markdown report table.

### B3 — README publishes an accuracy claim the suite does not produce

`benchmarks/README.md:172` asserts:

> **85%+ GA accuracy** demonstrates trust model effectiveness

The measured value is 75.0% today and 74.0% after B1 is fixed. No principled
decay constant reaches 85%.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml` states a decay formula for which
      `recency_factor(age = half_life) == 0.5`, and `half_life` is set to the
      value that reproduces the previously validated curve (`P10D`)
- [ ] `benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py` implements the same
      corrected formula, and a test asserts `recency_weight(half_life) == 0.5`
      to within 1e-9
- [ ] `benchmarks/fixtures/mock_apis.json` `temporal_decay.half_life_hours`
      agrees with the schema
- [ ] `python benchmarks/runner.py --scenario conflicting_sources` reports
      `accuracy_improvement_percent` as a value near `+63%`, not `+6304%`
- [ ] A test asserts that a `*_percent` metric is not re-scaled by the
      formatter
- [ ] `benchmarks/README.md` contains no unverified hardcoded accuracy claim
- [ ] `python benchmarks/runner.py --report` and `pytest benchmarks/tests/`
      both pass

## Verification Commands

```bash
pytest benchmarks/tests/ -v
python benchmarks/runner.py --scenario conflicting_sources
python -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml'))"
grep -c '85%+' benchmarks/README.md   # expect 0
ruff check benchmarks/ && mypy grounded_agency/
```

## Non-goals

- Redesigning the `conflicting_sources` ground-truth generator
- Applying `decay_model.min_trust` (currently declared but never enforced) —
  tracked separately
- Adding a validator for `authority_trust_model.yaml` — no validator covers any
  canonical schema from spec section 6.1 today; tracked separately

## Blocks

Blocks #104, which proposes extending the same trust model. The RFC for #104
should reason about a correct decay curve.

    """Regression tests for the authority trust model's decay curve.

    Issue #105: ``recency_factor`` was written as ``exp(-age/half_life)``,
    which yields 0.368 at ``age == half_life`` rather than 0.5, making the

        """The defining property of a half-life: f(half_life) == 0.5."""
        from benchmarks.scenarios.conflicting_sources import (
            _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS,
            _recency_weight,
        )

        assert _recency_weight(_TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS) == pytest.approx(0.5, abs=1e-9)

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
For the formatter, the real defect is that `_format_metrics` infers the *unit* from a substring match on the key name (`"improvement" in key`). That heuristic can't distinguish `accuracy_improvement_absolute` (a fraction, 0.29) from `accuracy_improvement_percent` (already scaled, 63.04) — both contain `"improvement"`. The fix isn't to add another substring; it's to make the `_percent` suffix authoritative and check it *first*, so the naming convention carries the unit rather than the guesswork.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

helper = '''def _is_fractional_metric(key: str) -> bool:
    """Whether a float metric is a 0-1 fraction that should render as a percentage.

    Keys suffixed ``_percent`` already carry a 0-100 value and must not be
    rescaled again; the ``_percent`` suffix is authoritative and is therefore
    checked before the substring heuristics (issue #105).
    """
    if key.endswith("_percent"):
        return False
    return "rate" in key or "accuracy" in key or "improvement" in key


def _render_float(key: str, value: float) -> str:
    """Render a float metric with the unit implied by its key."""
    if key.endswith("_percent"):
        return f"{value:.1f}%"
    if _is_fractional_metric(key):
        return f"{value:.1%}"
    return f"{value:.2f}"


'''

# Insert helpers immediately before _format_metrics
anchor = "def _format_metrics("
assert anchor in s

                f"+{improvement_val:.1%}"
                if isinstance(improvement_val, float)

fix(trust): correct decay to a true half-life and stop double-scaling percent metrics

Closes #105.

Three related defects caused the project to publish numbers that did not
mean what they said.

B1 — `decay_model.half_life` was an exponential time constant, not a
half-life. `recency_factor: exp(-age/half_life)` returns 0.3679 at
`age == half_life`, so the curve decayed 1/ln(2) ~ 1.44x faster than the
declared 14 days implied. Since `exp(-a/336h)` is identical to
`0.5**(a/H)` at `H = 336*ln2 = 232.9h = 9.70 days`, the declared `P14D`
was always a mislabelled ~9.7-day half-life. The formula is now
`0.5 ** (age/half_life)` and `half_life` is `P10D`, reproducing the curve
the benchmark suite actually validated rather than silently changing it.

  conflicting_sources GA accuracy: 75.0% -> 74.0%

B2 — `accuracy_improvement_percent` already carries a 0-100 value, but the
reporter formatted every key containing "improvement" with `:.1%`,
multiplying by 100 again and printing a +63% improvement as +6304.3%. The
`_percent` suffix is now authoritative and checked before the substring
heuristics. Callers that only render improvement deltas opt into treating
unsuffixed keys as fractions, so no other metric's rendering changes.

  accuracy_improvement_percent: +6304.3% -> +60.9%

B3 — `benchmarks/README.md` asserted "85%+ GA accuracy", which the suite
has never produced. Replaced with the command that reports the measured
figure, so the claim cannot go stale again.

Also corrects every document that asserted a 14-day half-life or published
the `exp(-age/half_life)` formula, including the ISO 42001, EU AI Act and
NIST AI RMF compliance artifacts, and a NIST profile reference to an
`unverified: 0.20` trust source that does not exist in the schema.

Verification: 888 tests pass; ruff, ruff format and mypy clean; ontology,
workflow, profile, skill-ref and benchmark-dep validators pass; conformance
suite passes.

cat > "$SP/i_minfloor.md" <<'EOF'
## Problem

`schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml` declares a trust floor:

```yaml
decay_model:
  half_life: P10D
  min_trust: 0.25
```

Nothing reads it. `grep -rn "min_trust" grounded_agency/ benchmarks/` returns
only `coordination/evidence_bridge.py`, which implements a **different** trust
concept (propagated `AgentDescriptor.trust_score` between agents) and whose
`min_trust_floor` defaults to `0.0`, not `0.25`.

`benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py::_recency_weight` returns
`0.5 ** (hours_ago / half_life)` with no clamp, so the recency factor decays
asymptotically to 0. `benchmarks/fixtures/mock_apis.json` carries an equally
unused `"min_weight": 0.25`.

## Why this matters beyond the code

Four compliance artifacts cite the floor as an implemented control, and one
uses it to justify a residual-risk rating:

| File | Claim |
|---|---|
| `docs/compliance/eu-ai-act/annex_iv_technical_documentation.md:304` | "Stale data influence \| Trust decay (τ₁/₂ = 10d), **minimum trust floor (0.25)** \| **Low** — mathematical decay ensures bounded staleness" |
| `docs/compliance/eu-ai-act/annex_iv_technical_documentation.md:269` | "τ₁/₂ = 10d, **floor = 0.25**" |
| `docs/compliance/eu-ai-act/quality_management_system.md:79` | "halves every 10 days, **floor 0.25**" |
| `docs/compliance/iso42001/risk_treatment_plan.md:56` | "**min trust floor 0.25**" |
| `docs/GROUNDED_AGENCY.md:376` | "Trust never decays below a minimum threshold of 0.25." |

"Bounded staleness" is precisely the property an unenforced floor does not
provide. The residual-risk rating of **Low** rests on a control that does not
exist in the reference implementation.

## Design question to settle first

`min_trust` is declared under `decay_model`, but the trust score is a product:

```
score = trust_weight(source) * confidence * recency_factor
```

It is ambiguous whether the floor clamps `recency_factor`, the product, or the
post-decay source weight. Each choice yields different conflict-resolution
behaviour and different benchmark numbers. The spec (§8.1) does not say.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `spec/STANDARD-v1.0.0.md` §8 states unambiguously what `min_trust` clamps
- [ ] The reference implementation enforces the floor per that definition
- [ ] A test asserts the floor holds as `age → ∞`
- [ ] The compliance artifacts above are either substantiated by the
      implementation or reworded, and the Annex IV residual-risk rating is
      re-derived from whatever is actually enforced
- [ ] `benchmarks/fixtures/mock_apis.json` `min_weight` agrees with the schema
      or is removed

## Verification Commands

```bash
pytest benchmarks/tests/ tests/ -v
python benchmarks/runner.py --scenario conflicting_sources
grep -rn "min_trust" grounded_agency/ benchmarks/    # must show enforcement
```

## Context

Found while fixing #105. Deliberately excluded from that PR because enforcing
the floor is a semantic change requiring a spec decision, not a defect fix.
EOF

## Problem

`spec/STANDARD-v1.0.0.md` §6.1 designates five **canonical schemas** that
conformant implementations depend on:

| Schema | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `world_state_schema.yaml` | World state structure |
| `event_schema.yaml` | Event and observation structure |
| `entity_taxonomy.yaml` | Entity type hierarchy |
| `authority_trust_model.yaml` | Trust scoring configuration |
| `identity_resolution_policy.yaml` | Identity resolution rules |

**No validator covers any of them.** CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs:

```
validate_ontology.py      -> capability_ontology.yaml
validate_workflows.py     -> workflow_catalog.yaml + schemas/workflows/
validate_profiles.py      -> schemas/profiles/
validate_skill_refs.py    -> skills/
validate_benchmark_deps.py-> benchmarks/
```

Nothing parses, shape-checks, or cross-references the §6.1 five. They are
loaded at runtime by consumers (`benchmarks/scenarios/conflicting_sources.py`,
`tools/sync_skill_schemas.py`) that assume a shape no test asserts.

## Evidence this gap has already cost the project

Every defect in #105 and #106 lived in `authority_trust_model.yaml` or in
documents describing it, and every one shipped through CI green:

- `recency_factor` was mathematically inconsistent with the `half_life` field
  name it referenced (#105)
- `benchmarks/fixtures/mock_apis.json` drifted from the schema's `half_life`
  and nothing noticed (#105)
- `decay_model.min_trust` is declared and never enforced (#106)

#104 proposes adding an `agent_reliability_profile` block to the trust model.
Adding fields to a file that nothing validates means the new block ships with
no automatable check — which means an acceptance criterion for #104 has no
verification command, and the Spec Validation Gate cannot pass.

- [ ] `tools/validate_canonical_schemas.py` exists and validates all five §6.1

      `schema.version` / `schema.description` header, and matches a declared

- [ ] Every source in `source_ranking.default_order` has a weight, and vice

- [ ] `CLAUDE.md` documents the new command alongside the other validators

- Converting the canonical schemas to JSON Schema

You've overridden my recommendation on the floor — proceeding with the full implementation. First I need to settle the semantics I flagged as ambiguous, and the evidence does point one way:

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Three independent signals say `min_trust` clamps the **recency factor**, not the product or the source weight:
1. It is declared *inside* `decay_model`, adjacent to `half_life` — the block that governs decay, not scoring.
2. The benchmark fixture's own name for it is `temporal_decay.min_weight` (`mock_apis.json:38`) — the *decay weight*.
3. `docs/GROUNDED_AGENCY.md:376` reads "Trust never **decays** below…" — decay is the operation being floored.

So: `recency_factor = max(0.5 ** (age/half_life), min_trust)`. The floor is reached at exactly 2 half-lives (`0.5² = 0.25`), i.e. decay stops at 20 days — a coherent reading. I'll document that derivation in the schema so the next reader doesn't have to re-derive it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

_LOW_TRUST_TYPES = ["observability_pipeline", "derived_inference", "human_note"]

_TRUST_MODEL_PATH = (
    Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "schemas" / "authority_trust_model.yaml"
)


def _load_trust_model() -> tuple[dict[str, float], int]:
    """Load trust weights and decay settings from authority_trust_model.yaml."""
    if not _TRUST_MODEL_PATH.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Trust model not found: {_TRUST_MODEL_PATH}. "
            "Benchmark integrity requires this file."
        )

    model = safe_yaml_load(_TRUST_MODEL_PATH)
    weights = model.get("source_ranking", {}).get("weights", {})
    half_life_str = model.get("decay_model", {}).get("half_life", "P10D")
    match = re.fullmatch(r"P(\d+)D", half_life_str)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported half_life format '{half_life_str}'. Expected 'P<n>D'."
        )
    half_life_hours = int(match.group(1)) * 24
    return weights, half_life_hours


_TRUST_WEIGHTS, _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS = _load_trust_model()


def _recency_weight(
    hours_ago: float, half_life: float = _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS
) -> float:
    """Weight an observation by age using true half-life decay.

    Returns exactly 0.5 at ``hours_ago == half_life``.  The earlier form
    ``exp(-hours_ago / half_life)`` treated ``half_life`` as an exponential
    time constant, decaying 1/ln(2) ~ 1.44x too fast (issue #105).
    """
    return 0.5 ** (hours_ago / half_life)


class ConflictingSourcesScenario(BenchmarkScenario):
    """Benchmark for conflicting data source resolution."""

    name = "conflicting_sources"
    description = "Tests trust-weighted conflict resolution vs last-write-wins"

    def __init__(self, seed: int = 42, verbose: bool = False, num_cases: int = 100):
        super().__init__(seed, verbose)
        self.num_cases = num_cases
        self.test_cases: list[dict] = []

    def setup(self) -> None:
        """Generate test cases with known ground truth.

        ~60% of cases favor source1 (high-trust, correct value),
        ~40% favor source2 (low-trust but very recent).
        """
        random.seed(self.seed)
        self.test_cases = []

        for i in range(self.num_cases):
            source1_type = random.choice(_HIGH_TRUST_TYPES)
            source2_type = random.choice(_LOW_TRUST_TYPES)

            # Ground truth: random value A or B
            ground_truth = random.choice(["A", "B"])

            # ~60% chance source1 has the correct value (trust advantage)
            if random.random() < 0.6:
                # Source1 correct: high-trust + correct → GA picks source1

def _load_trust_model() -> tuple[dict[str, float], int, float]:
    """Load trust weights and decay settings from authority_trust_model.yaml."""
    if not _TRUST_MODEL_PATH.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(

            "Benchmark integrity requires this file."
        )

    model = safe_yaml_load(_TRUST_MODEL_PATH)
    weights = model.get("source_ranking", {}).get("weights", {})
    decay = model.get("decay_model", {})
    half_life_str = decay.get("half_life", "P10D")
    match = re.fullmatch(r"P(\d+)D", half_life_str)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported half_life format '{half_life_str}'. Expected 'P<n>D'."
        )
    half_life_hours = int(match.group(1)) * 24
    min_trust = float(decay.get("min_trust", 0.0))
    if not 0.0 <= min_trust <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"min_trust must be in [0.0, 1.0], got {min_trust}")
    return weights, half_life_hours, min_trust


_TRUST_WEIGHTS, _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS, _TRUST_MIN = _load_trust_model()


def _recency_weight(
    hours_ago: float,
    half_life: float = _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS,
    min_trust: float = _TRUST_MIN,
) -> float:
    """Weight an observation by age using floored half-life decay.

    Returns exactly 0.5 at ``hours_ago == half_life``.  The earlier form
    ``exp(-hours_ago / half_life)`` treated ``half_life`` as an exponential
    time constant, decaying 1/ln(2) ~ 1.44x too fast (issue #105).

    Decay stops at ``decay_model.min_trust``, so an observation never becomes
    worthless purely through age -- it only ever loses its recency advantage
    over fresher ones.  With the shipped values the floor is reached at exactly
    two half-lives (``0.5**2 == 0.25``).  This clamp was declared in the schema
    but unimplemented until issue #106.
    """
    return max(0.5 ** (hours_ago / half_life), min_trust)

    half_life: float = _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS,
    min_trust: float = _TRUST_MIN,

    """Weight an observation by age using floored half-life decay.

    Returns exactly 0.5 at ``hours_ago == half_life``.  The earlier form
    ``exp(-hours_ago / half_life)`` treated ``half_life`` as an exponential
    time constant, decaying 1/ln(2) ~ 1.44x too fast (issue #105).

    Decay stops at ``decay_model.min_trust``, so an observation never becomes
    worthless purely through age -- it only ever loses its recency advantage
    over fresher ones.  With the shipped values the floor is reached at exactly
    two half-lives (``0.5**2 == 0.25``).  This clamp was declared in the schema
    but unimplemented until issue #106.
    """

"""
Scenario 1: Conflicting Sources

Tests whether Grounded Agency's trust-weighted conflict resolution
produces more accurate results than naive last-write-wins.

Setup:
- Two mock APIs return different values for the same entity
- Ground truth is known for each test case
- Baseline uses last response received
- GA uses trust weights and timestamps

Metrics:
- Accuracy: Correctness compared to ground truth
- Consistency: Same result on repeated runs
- Evidence: Completeness of audit trail
"""

import random
import re
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from grounded_agency.state.evidence_store import EvidenceAnchor, EvidenceStore
from grounded_agency.utils.safe_yaml import safe_yaml_load

from .base import BenchmarkScenario

_HIGH_TRUST_TYPES = ["hardware_sensor", "system_of_record", "primary_api"]
_LOW_TRUST_TYPES = ["observability_pipeline", "derived_inference", "human_note"]

_TRUST_MODEL_PATH = (
    Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "schemas" / "authority_trust_model.yaml"
)


def _load_trust_model() -> tuple[dict[str, float], int]:
    """Load trust weights and decay settings from authority_trust_model.yaml."""
    if not _TRUST_MODEL_PATH.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Trust model not found: {_TRUST_MODEL_PATH}. "
            "Benchmark integrity requires this file."
        )

    model = safe_yaml_load(_TRUST_MODEL_PATH)
    weights = model.get("source_ranking", {}).get("weights", {})
    half_life_str = model.get("decay_model", {}).get("half_life", "P10D")
    match = re.fullmatch(r"P(\d+)D", half_life_str)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unsupported half_life format '{half_life_str}'. Expected 'P<n>D'."
        )
    half_life_hours = int(match.group(1)) * 24
    return weights, half_life_hours


_TRUST_WEIGHTS, _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS = _load_trust_model()


def _recency_weight(
    hours_ago: float, half_life: float = _TRUST_HALF_LIFE_HOURS
) -> float:
    """Weight an observation by age using true half-life decay.

    Returns exactly 0.5 at ``hours_ago == half_life``.  The earlier form
    ``exp(-hours_ago / half_life)`` treated ``half_life`` as an exponential
    time constant, decaying 1/ln(2) ~ 1.44x too fast (issue #105).
    """
    return 0.5 ** (hours_ago / half_life)


class ConflictingSourcesScenario(BenchmarkScenario):
    """Benchmark for conflicting data source resolution."""

    name = "conflicting_sources"
    description = "Tests trust-weighted conflict resolution vs last-write-wins"

    def __init__(self, seed: int = 42, verbose: bool = False, num_cases: int = 100):
        super().__init__(seed, verbose)
        self.num_cases = num_cases
        self.test_cases: list[dict] = []

    def setup(self) -> None:
        """Generate test cases with known ground truth.

        ~60% of cases favor source1 (high-trust, correct value),
        ~40% favor source2 (low-trust but very recent).
        """
        random.seed(self.seed)
        self.test_cases = []

        for i in range(self.num_cases):
            source1_type = random.choice(_HIGH_TRUST_TYPES)
            source2_type = random.choice(_LOW_TRUST_TYPES)

            # Ground truth: random value A or B
            ground_truth = random.choice(["A", "B"])

            # ~60% chance source1 has the correct value (trust advantage)
            if random.random() < 0.6:
                # Source1 correct: high-trust + correct → GA picks source1
                source1_value = ground_truth
                source2_value = "B" if ground_truth == "A" else "A"
                source1_hours_ago = random.uniform(1, 48)
                source2_hours_ago = random.uniform(1, 72)
            else:
                # Source2 correct: low-trust but very recent → recency helps
                source1_value = "B" if ground_truth == "A" else "A"
                source2_value = ground_truth
                # Source1 is stale, source2 is very recent
                source1_hours_ago = random.uniform(24, 168)
                source2_hours_ago = random.uniform(0.1, 2)

            self.test_cases.append(
                {
                    "id": i,
                    "ground_truth": ground_truth,
                    "source1": {
                        "value": source1_value,
                        "type": source1_type,
                        "hours_ago": source1_hours_ago,
                    },
                    "source2": {
                        "value": source2_value,
                        "type": source2_type,
                        "hours_ago": source2_hours_ago,
                    },
                }
            )

        self.log(f"Generated {len(self.test_cases)} test cases")

    def run_baseline(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Baseline: Last-write-wins (or first, randomly chosen).

        This simulates naive approaches that don't consider
        source reliability or timestamps.
        """
        random.seed(self.seed + 1)  # Different seed for baseline randomness

        correct = 0
        results = []

        for case in self.test_cases:
            # Randomly pick which source "wins" (simulates race condition)
            winner = random.choice(["source1", "source2"])
            selected = case[winner]["value"]

            is_correct = selected == case["ground_truth"]
            if is_correct:
                correct += 1

            results.append(
                {
                    "case_id": case["id"],
                    "selected": selected,
                    "correct": is_correct,
                    "evidence_anchors": [],  # No evidence tracking
                }
            )

        accuracy = correct / len(self.test_cases)
        self.log(f"Baseline accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}")

        return {
            "accuracy": accuracy,
            "correct_count": correct,
            "total_count": len(self.test_cases),
            "has_evidence": False,
            "results": results,
        }

    def run_ga(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Grounded Agency: Trust-weighted resolution with EvidenceStore.

        Uses source trust weights and temporal recency to
        select the most reliable value. Evidence anchors are
        tracked through the real EvidenceStore.
        """
        evidence_store = EvidenceStore(max_anchors=self.num_cases * 2)
        correct = 0
        results = []

        for case in self.test_cases:
            # Calculate scores for each source
            s1 = case["source1"]
            s2 = case["source2"]

            score1 = _TRUST_WEIGHTS[s1["type"]] * _recency_weight(s1["hours_ago"])
            score2 = _TRUST_WEIGHTS[s2["type"]] * _recency_weight(s2["hours_ago"])

            # Select higher-scoring source
            if score1 >= score2:
                selected = s1["value"]
                winning_source = "source1"
            else:
                selected = s2["value"]
                winning_source = "source2"

            is_correct = selected == case["ground_truth"]
            if is_correct:
                correct += 1

            # Create evidence anchor via EvidenceStore
            anchor = EvidenceAnchor.from_tool_output(
                tool_name="retrieve",
                tool_use_id=f"conflict_resolution_{case['id']}",
                tool_input={
                    "source": winning_source,
                    "source_type": case[winning_source]["type"],
                },
            )
            evidence_store.add_anchor(anchor, capability_id="retrieve")

            results.append(
                {
                    "case_id": case["id"],
                    "selected": selected,
                    "correct": is_correct,
                    "evidence_anchors": [anchor.to_dict()],
                    "score_source1": score1,
                    "score_source2": score2,
                }
            )

        accuracy = correct / len(self.test_cases)
        evidence_count = len(evidence_store)

        self.log(f"GA accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}")
        self.log(f"Evidence anchors collected: {evidence_count}")

        return {
            "accuracy": accuracy,
            "correct_count": correct,
            "total_count": len(self.test_cases),
            "has_evidence": True,
            "evidence_completeness": 1.0,  # All decisions have evidence
            "results": results,
        }

    def compare(
        self, baseline_result: dict[str, Any], ga_result: dict[str, Any]
    ) -> dict[str, float]:
        """Compare accuracy and evidence completeness."""
        accuracy_improvement = ga_result["accuracy"] - baseline_result["accuracy"]
        accuracy_improvement_pct = (
            (accuracy_improvement / baseline_result["accuracy"]) * 100
            if baseline_result["accuracy"] > 0
            else 100
        )

        comparison = {
            "accuracy_improvement_absolute": accuracy_improvement,
            "accuracy_improvement_percent": accuracy_improvement_pct,
            "evidence_completeness": ga_result.get("evidence_completeness", 0),
        }

        self.log(f"Accuracy improvement: +{accuracy_improvement:.2%}")
        self.log(
            f"Evidence completeness: {ga_result.get('evidence_completeness', 0):.0%}"
        )

        return comparison

def _render_float(key: str, value: float, *, default_is_fraction: bool = False) -> str:
    """Render a float metric with the unit implied by its key.

    ``default_is_fraction`` is set by callers that only ever render
    improvement deltas, which are 0-1 fractions unless the key says
    otherwise.
    """
    if key.endswith("_percent"):
        return f"{value:.1f}%"
    if default_is_fraction or _is_fractional_metric(key):
        return f"{value:.1%}"
    return f"{value:.2f}"

input.new_string:
``default_is_fraction`` is set by callers that only ever render
    improvement deltas, which are 0-1 fractions unless the key says
    otherwise.

    A value outside [-1, 1] is never a fraction whatever its key suggests, so
    it is rendered as a plain number.  ``_get_primary_metric`` falls back to
    the first key in a metrics dict, which can be an absolute count such as
    ``compute_savings``; without this guard 3600.0 would render as 360000.0%.
    """
    if key.endswith("_percent"):
        return f"{value:.1f}%"
    if (default_is_fraction or _is_fractional_metric(key)) and -1.0 <= value <= 1.0:
        return f"{value:.1%}"
    return f"{value:.2f}"

cat > "$SP/pr.md" <<'EOF'
Closes #105. Closes #106.

The authority trust model published numbers that did not mean what they said,
and four compliance artifacts cited a control that did not exist.

## What was wrong

**The decay was not a half-life.** `recency_factor: exp(-age/half_life)`
returns `0.3679` at `age == half_life`, not `0.5` — `half_life` was being used
as an exponential time constant. The curve decayed `1/ln(2) ≈ 1.44x` faster
than the declared 14 days implied.

```
age=  0d   exp(-age/hl)=1.0000   0.5^(age/hl)=1.0000
age=  7d   exp(-age/hl)=0.6065   0.5^(age/hl)=0.7071
age= 14d   exp(-age/hl)=0.3679   0.5^(age/hl)=0.5000   <-- should be 0.5
age= 28d   exp(-age/hl)=0.1353   0.5^(age/hl)=0.2500
```

**A headline improvement figure was inflated 100x.**
`accuracy_improvement_percent` already carries a 0-100 value; the reporter
formatted every key containing `improvement` with `:.1%`. CI printed a +63%
improvement as **+6304.3%**.

**`decay_model.min_trust: 0.25` was read by nothing.** The recency factor
decayed asymptotically to zero, so the "bounded staleness" that the EU AI Act
Annex IV residual-risk table cites to justify a **Low** rating did not hold.

**The README asserted an accuracy the suite has never produced** — "85%+ GA
accuracy", against a measured 75.0%.

## Why `half_life` moves 14d -> 10d

`exp(-a/336h)` is *identical* to `0.5**(a/H)` at `H = 336·ln2 = 232.9h = 9.70
days`. The declared `P14D` was therefore always a mislabelled ~9.7-day
half-life. Setting `P10D` reproduces the curve the benchmark suite actually
validated rather than silently changing model behaviour under cover of a bug
fix. (`P10D` rather than `P9.7D` because the loader's `P(\d+)D` parser takes
whole days; the 3% residual is disclosed here rather than hidden.)

| Decay | GA accuracy |
|---|---|
| `exp(-a/336h)` — before | 75.0% |
| `0.5^(a/10d)` — after | **74.0%** |
| `0.5^(a/14d)` — formula fixed, label kept | 65.0% |

The 1pp difference is the parser rounding, not a modelling change.

## What changed

**Normative**
- `spec/STANDARD-v1.0.0.md` §8.1 now requires time decay to be a true
  half-life, and defines `min_trust` as a floor on the **decay factor** — not
  on the composed §8.2 score, and not on the static source weight
- `schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml`: `recency_factor` is
  `max(0.5 ** (age/half_life), min_trust)`; `half_life: P10D`
- `spec/CHANGELOG.md` records both under Unreleased

**Implementation**
- `_recency_weight` implements the floored half-life; the floor is reached at
  exactly two half-lives (`0.5² = 0.25`)
- All four metric-rendering paths route through one `_render_float`, which
  refuses the percentage form for any value outside `[-1, 1]`

**Documentation** — every artifact asserting a 14-day half-life or publishing
`exp(-age/half_life)`, including the ISO 42001, EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF
compliance documents; a NIST profile reference to a source `unverified: 0.20`
that does not exist in the schema; and the README's unverifiable accuracy
claim, replaced by the command that reports the measured figure.

## Semantics decision, recorded

The spec did not say what `min_trust` clamps. Three independent signals say the
decay factor, and §8.1 now states it:

1. It is declared inside `decay_model`, adjacent to `half_life`
2. The benchmark fixture names it `temporal_decay.min_weight`
3. `docs/GROUNDED_AGENCY.md` describes it as the bound below which trust never
   *decays*

## Verification

```
894 tests pass (pytest tests/ benchmarks/tests/)
ruff check / ruff format --check / mypy grounded_agency/   clean
7/7 validators pass
conformance suite passes
generated report contains no percentage of four digits or more
```

The floor is covered by unit tests rather than by scenario accuracy:
`conflicting_sources` generates ages up to 168h and the floor engages only past
480h, so enabling it does not move the benchmark.

## Follow-ups filed, not done here

- **#107** — no validator covers any of the five canonical schemas designated
  by §6.1. Every defect above lived in `authority_trust_model.yaml` or in
  documents describing it, and every one shipped through CI green. This blocks
  a clean Spec Validation Gate for #104.
EOF

The through-line across all of this: **every defect was a claim that nothing checked.** The decay formula contradicted its own field name; a fixture drifted from the schema it mirrors; a compliance artifact rated residual risk on an unimplemented control; a README published an accuracy the suite never produced; a NIST profile cited a trust source that doesn't exist. That's why #107 matters more than it looks. It isn't cleanup; it's the missing feedback loop that let five separate untrue statements accumulate in a standards document.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Decay is now a true half-life, `P10D` | ✅ `spec` §8.1 + schema + implementation |
| `min_trust` enforced and defined normatively | ✅ closes #106 |
| `+6304.3%` → `+60.9%`, all 4 render paths unified | ✅ |
| 11 docs + 4 compliance artifacts corrected | ✅ |
| Verification | 894 tests, ruff/format/mypy clean, 7/7 validators, conformance ✅ |

**Filed, not built:** [#106](https://github.com/synaptiai/agent-capability-standard/issues/106) (done in PR #108), [#107](https://github.com/synaptiai/agent-capability-standard/issues/107) (canonical schema validator).

**Pushed to `main`:** the `.gitignore` chore only, as you approved.

## What's next — #104's RFC

Your six decisions are locked and unchanged:

| Node | Decision |
|---|---|
| Deliverable | `spec/RFC-0002-agent-reliability-profile.md`, RFC-0001 shape |
| Model | New concept + name the missing first-class agent identity as prerequisite |
| Axes | All three, tiered by derivability (`delivery` derivable today; `calibration` needs a defined join; `adaptation` needs telemetry that doesn't exist) |
| Verification | New `tools/validate_rfcs.py` in CI |
| Citation | Prior art in RFC Motivation only, with the provenance caveat |

One sequencing question, since it changes what the RFC can promise.

"""
Tests for grounded_query() and GroundedClient wrappers.

Since claude_agent_sdk may not be installed in test environments,
these tests focus on:
- CostSummary dataclass behavior
- Adapter cost_summary initialization
- Import error handling
- Integration with adapter's wrap_options
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

import pytest

from grounded_agency import (
    CostSummary,
    GroundedAgentAdapter,
)

# =============================================================================
# CostSummary Tests
# =============================================================================


class TestCostSummary:
    """Tests for the CostSummary dataclass."""

    def test_default_values(self):
        """Test CostSummary initializes with zero values."""
        summary = CostSummary()
        assert summary.total_usd == 0.0
        assert summary.by_model == {}
        assert summary.turn_count == 0

    def test_update_cost(self):
        """Test updating cost values."""
        summary = CostSummary()
        summary.total_usd = 0.05
        summary.by_model["sonnet"] = 0.05
        summary.turn_count = 1

        assert summary.total_usd == 0.05
        assert summary.by_model["sonnet"] == 0.05
        assert summary.turn_count == 1

    def test_multiple_models(self):
        """Test tracking cost across multiple models."""
        summary = CostSummary()
        summary.by_model["sonnet"] = 0.03
        summary.by_model["haiku"] = 0.01
        summary.total_usd = 0.04

        assert len(summary.by_model) == 2
        assert summary.total_usd == 0.04

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The test isn't wrong in intent — its docstring and `except (ConnectionError, OSError, ValueError)` show it *deliberately* tolerates "no live API connection." The defect is that it doesn't enumerate the SDK's own error types, so an environment condition it means to swallow leaks through as a failure.

That matters because `CLAUDE.md` records a deliberate decision in #99 to "install real SDK, remove all mock/skip patterns." Adding a `skipif` would reverse that. Widening the `except` to the SDK's error base honors it — the test still runs, still asserts no `ImportError`.

While that runs — a status summary of where the whole engagement stands.

## Current state

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| **PR [#108](https://github.com/synaptiai/agent-capability-standard/pull/108)** — #105 + #106 | Open, CI red on two **pre-existing** failures, both now fixed locally |
| **#107** — canonical schema validator | Filed; you chose to build it **before** the #104 RFC |
| **#104** — `agent_reliability_profile` RFC | Not started; all six design decisions locked |

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The CI failures were both **toolchain drift, not my changes** — proven by the `.gitignore`-only commit on `main` failing identically. Two independent unpinned-dependency traps:

1. **`pip install -e ".[dev]"` installs unpinned `ruff`.** CI got 0.16.5, which formats Python code blocks *inside Markdown*; my local 0.14.14 does not. So `benchmarks/README.md:142` — a code sample missing PEP 8's two blank lines before a class — became a hard CI failure with no code change at all.
2. **`claude-agent-sdk` is unpinned too.** CI got 0.2.148 which raises `ResultError`; my local 0.1.25 doesn't have that class. `tests/test_grounded_query.py` already *intended* to tolerate "no live API connection" but enumerated only `(ConnectionError, OSError, ValueError)` — so the SDK's own error escaped.

I verified the fix rather than assuming it: installed 0.2.148 in a scratch venv and confirmed `ResultError` and `ProcessError` both subclass `ClaudeSDKError`. Catching the base honors #99's "no mocks/skips" decision instead of reversing it with a `skipif`.

The deeper point is the same one #107 makes: **this repo has no mechanism that would catch either drift before CI.** Green locally ≠ green in CI when the toolchain floats.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Domain profile validator: validates profiles against profile_schema.yaml

This validator ensures all domain profiles conform to the profile schema,
catching configuration errors early and maintaining consistency.

Validates:
1) Required fields are present (domain, version, trust_weights, etc.)
2) Trust weight values are between 0.0 and 1.0
3) Enum values match allowed values (risk thresholds, checkpoint policies)
4) Semantic version format for version field
5) Source types match allowed enum values

Usage:
- python3 tools/validate_profiles.py
- python3 tools/validate_profiles.py --verbose

"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

import yaml
from yaml_util import YAMLSizeExceededError, safe_yaml_load

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
PROFILES_DIR = ROOT / "schemas" / "profiles"


# -------------------- Schema Constants --------------------

REQUIRED_FIELDS = [
    "domain",
    "version",
    "trust_weights",
    "risk_thresholds",
    "checkpoint_policy",
    "evidence_policy",
]

RISK_AUTO_APPROVE_ENUM = ["none", "low", "medium", "high"]
RISK_REQUIRE_REVIEW_ENUM = ["low", "medium", "high"]
RISK_REQUIRE_HUMAN_ENUM = ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]
CHECKPOINT_POLICY_ENUM = ["always", "high_risk", "medium_risk", "never"]
SOURCE_TYPE_ENUM = ["api", "sensor", "database", "human", "document", "system_log"]

VERSION_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$")


# -------------------- Validation Functions --------------------


def validate_required_fields(profile: dict[str, Any], errors: list[str], name: str) -> None:
    """Check that all required fields are present."""
    for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS:
        if field not in profile:
            errors.append(f"[{name}] Missing required field: '{field}'")


def validate_version_format(profile: dict[str, Any], errors: list[str], name: str) -> None:
    """Check version follows semantic versioning pattern."""
    version = profile.get("version")
    if version is not None:
        if not isinstance(version, str):
            errors.append(f"[{name}] Field 'version' must be a string, got {type(version).__name__}")

content.text:
CI's lint/format now passes — the fix worked. Meanwhile, designing #107 surfaced something bigger than drift between files.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**The spec's normative field tables and the canonical schemas are different vocabularies.**

§6.2 says observations MUST record seven fields. Only two match `ObservationEvent` in `world_state_schema.yaml`:

| §6.2 says MUST | Schema actually has |
|---|---|
| `id` | `event_id` |
| `timestamp` | ✅ `timestamp` |
| `source` | ✅ `source` |
| `raw_payload` + `canonical_payload` | `payload` (one field, not two) |
| `evidence_anchors` | `anchors` |
| `provenance` | **absent** |

§6.3 is the same story: `version_id` and `lineage` are marked Required=Yes in the spec but sit as *optional* properties under `meta`, and `timestamp` doesn't exist at all — the schema calls it `meta.as_of`.

An implementer reading §6.2 and an implementer reading `world_state_schema.yaml` would build incompatible systems. This is the exact failure the standard exists to prevent, sitting inside the standard.

It also directly shapes #107: a validator that checks the schemas against the spec **fails on day one**, and fixing it is normative work — not validator work.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

questions.question: What should `tools/validate_canonical_schemas.py` enforce, given that spec §6.2/§6.3 field tables do not match the schemas they describe?

options.label: Structural + internal + cross-file; spec-conformance as warnings (Recommended)
options.description: Enforce as errors: the shared `schema.{name,version,description}` header, per-file invariants (source_ranking symmetry, field_authority sources exist, half_life format, thresholds ordered), and cross-file agreement with mock_apis.json. Report §6.2/§6.3 mismatches as non-fatal warnings, exactly like validate_profiles.py's SEC-009 trust-calibration warnings. Ships green, catches every #105-class defect, and surfaces the vocabulary gap without blocking.

options.label: Structural + internal + cross-file only
options.description: Errors for everything mechanically checkable within and between schema files; no spec-text comparison at all. Smallest, cleanest validator. Leaves the §6.2/§6.3 divergence entirely undetected — which is the largest correctness gap I have found in this repo.

options.label: Full spec conformance as errors, reconcile the schemas
options.description: The validator asserts §6.2/§6.3 verbatim and I reconcile schema and spec so it passes: rename or add `id`/`raw_payload`/`canonical_payload`/`evidence_anchors`/`provenance`, promote `version_id`/`lineage` to required. Correct destination, but a MAJOR breaking schema change per §11.4 — far beyond a validator issue.

content.text:
Verified conclusively. Bringing this back with the correction.

## Correction to what I told you

I compared §6.2 against the wrong type. `provenance` is **not** absent, and `raw`/`canonical` are **not** collapsed into one field — I was reading `world_state.types.ObservationEvent` (the narrow projection into world state) instead of `event_schema.yaml`'s `event`, which is what §6.2 actually describes. Six of the seven §6.2 fields are already in `required` there.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
There are **two deliberate vocabularies** in this repo, and §6.2's prose sits in neither:

| Layer | Vocabulary | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| Capability I/O | `evidence_anchors` | 72× in `capability_ontology.yaml` |
| Canonical event | `event_id`, `raw`, `canonical`, `anchors`, `provenance` | `event_schema.yaml`, `world_state_schema.yaml`, `transform_mapping_rawlog_to_observation.yaml`, ~190 files |

§6.2's table mixes them: it borrows `evidence_anchors` from the capability layer, and invents `raw_payload`/`canonical_payload` — names that appear in **zero** schema files. The transform mapping, which is the actual normative bridge, writes `canonical_event.raw` and `canonical_event.canonical`.

So the schemas are self-consistent and consistent with 190 dependents. The prose is the outlier.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

What's actually broken, separated by size:

| # | Finding | Real gap? | Cost to fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prose names ≠ schema names (`id`/`raw_payload`/`canonical_payload`/`evidence_anchors`) | **No** — functional parity | PATCH clarification, ~10 lines |
| 2 | `provenance` declared but not `required` in `event_schema.event` | **Yes** — §6.2 says MUST | 1 line |
| 3 | `version_id`, `lineage` optional under `world_state.meta` | **Yes** — §6.3 says MUST | 2 lines |
| 4 | §6.3's `timestamp` is the schema's `meta.as_of` | No — naming | part of #1 |

I checked the fixture risk advisor raised: **no conformance fixture constructs events or world state** — all 25 are `workflow_catalog.yaml` files. So promoting those three fields breaks nothing in-repo, though it is still §11.4-breaking for external implementers.

Your validator-scope answer survives this correction intact — "full spec conformance as errors" *works* once the prose is accurate and those three fields are required. That's the version of your choice that can actually pass CI.

# ─── Canonical Schema Validator ───


class TestValidateCanonicalSchemas:
    """Tests for tools/validate_canonical_schemas.py (issue #107).

    STANDARD-v1.0.0 §6.1 designates five canonical schemas. Until this
    validator existed nothing checked them, so the defects in #105 and #106 all
    shipped through a green CI. The negative cases below reproduce those exact
    defects to prove the validator would now catch them.
    """

    SCHEMAS = ROOT / "schemas"

    def _assert_drift_is_caught(
        self, relative_path: str, old: str, new: str
    ) -> None:
        """Inject a defect, assert the validator fails, always restore."""
        path = ROOT / relative_path
        original = path.read_text()
        assert old in original, f"anchor not found in {relative_path}: {old!r}"
        try:
            path.write_text(original.replace(old, new, 1))
            result = run_validator("validate_canonical_schemas.py")
            assert result.returncode != 0, (
                f"validator passed despite injected drift in {relative_path}"
            )
            assert "FAIL" in result.stdout
        finally:
            path.write_text(original)

    def test_passes_with_current_schemas(self) -> None:
        result = run_validator("validate_canonical_schemas.py")
        assert result.returncode == 0, result.stdout + result.stderr
        assert "PASS" in result.stdout

    def test_verbose_flag_lists_every_canonical_schema(self) -> None:
        result = run_validator("validate_canonical_schemas.py", ["--verbose"])
        assert result.returncode == 0
        for name in (
            "world_state_schema",
            "event_schema",
            "entity_taxonomy",
            "authority_trust_model",
            "identity_resolution_policy",
        ):
            assert name in result.stdout

    def test_catches_exponential_decay_regression(self) -> None:
        """Issue #105: exp(-age/half_life) is not a half-life."""
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml",
            "recency_factor: max(0.5 ** (age/half_life), min_trust)",
            "recency_factor: exp(-age/half_life)",
        )

    def test_catches_benchmark_fixture_drift(self) -> None:
        """Issue #105: mock_apis.json silently disagreed with the schema."""
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml",
            "half_life: P10D",
            "half_life: P14D",
        )

    def test_catches_phantom_field_authority_source(self) -> None:
        """Issue #105: the NIST profile cited a source that never existed."""
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml",
            "    - hardware_sensor\n    - system_of_record",
            "    - unverified\n    - system_of_record",
        )

    def test_catches_source_ranking_asymmetry(self) -> None:
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml",
            "    human_note: 0.55",
            "    human_note: 0.55\n    ghost_source: 0.5",
        )

    def test_catches_out_of_range_min_trust(self) -> None:
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/authority_trust_model.yaml",
            "min_trust: 0.25",
            "min_trust: 25",
        )

    def test_catches_missing_spec_6_2_required_field(self) -> None:
        """STANDARD §6.2 lists provenance as MUST."""
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/event_schema.yaml",
            "  - provenance\n  properties:\n    event_id:",
            "  properties:\n    event_id:",
        )

    def test_catches_missing_spec_6_3_required_field(self) -> None:
        """STANDARD §6.3 lists snapshot lineage as MUST."""
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/world_state_schema.yaml",
            "      - version_id\n      - lineage",
            "      - version_id",
        )

    def test_catches_unordered_alias_thresholds(self) -> None:
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/identity_resolution_policy.yaml",
            "auto_merge: 0.9",
            "auto_merge: 0.5",
        )

    def test_catches_malformed_schema_version(self) -> None:
        self._assert_drift_is_caught(
            "schemas/entity_taxonomy.yaml",
            "  version: 1.0.0",
            "  version: v1",
        )

    def test_catches_missing_canonical_schema_file(self) -> None:
        """STANDARD §6.1 requires all five files to be present."""
        path = self.SCHEMAS / "entity_taxonomy.yaml"
        moved = self.SCHEMAS / "_entity_taxonomy.moved"
        path.rename(moved)
        try:
            result = run_validator("validate_canonical_schemas.py")
            assert result.returncode != 0
            assert "§6.1" in result.stdout
        finally:
            moved.rename(path)
PY

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
`sync_skill_schemas.py` is **not idempotent**. Its comment rewrite maps `schemas/workflows/` → `(repo-level) schemas/workflows/`, and re-running it applies the rewrite to already-rewritten text:

```
-#   - (repo-level) schemas/workflows/manufacturing_workflows.yaml
+#   - (repo-level) (repo-level) schemas/workflows/manufacturing_workflows.yaml
```

`CLAUDE.md` documents `python tools/sync_skill_schemas.py` as a standard command, so anyone following the project's own instructions corrupts these 17 files a little more each time. A sync tool must be idempotent — running it on a synced tree is meant to be a no-op, which is precisely what makes it safe to run in CI as a drift check.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

        """Re-running the sync on a synced tree must change nothing.

        The comment rewrite `schemas/workflows/` -> `(repo-level)
        schemas/workflows/` used to reapply itself to already-rewritten text,

            cwd=str(ROOT),
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,

Closes #107.

STANDARD-v1.0.0 §6.1 designates five canonical schemas that conformant
implementations depend on. No validator covered any of them: CI checked the
ontology, workflows, profiles and skill refs only. Every defect in #105 and
#106 lived in `authority_trust_model.yaml` or in documents describing it, and
every one shipped through a green CI.

`tools/validate_canonical_schemas.py` runs in the CI "Validate YAML schemas"
job and asserts eight families: file presence and the shared schema header;
§6.2 and §6.3 required fields; trust-model internal consistency (source
symmetry, weight ranges, field_authority sources, ISO-8601 half-life, and a
refusal of exp() in recency_factor); alias-threshold ordering; the entity id
convention; cross-file agreement with the benchmark fixture; and vendored
skill copies against their source.

Reconciling spec and schemas
----------------------------

§6.2 described observations with `id` / `raw_payload` / `canonical_payload` /
`evidence_anchors` -- names that appear in no schema file. The canonical event
in `event_schema.yaml` has always carried all seven fields as `event_id` /
`raw` / `canonical` / `anchors`, and the normative bridge
`transform_mapping_rawlog_to_observation.yaml` writes those names. §6.3
likewise placed snapshot identity at the top level where the schema keeps it
under `meta`. Both tables now name the real fields, and §6.2 states that the
canonical-event namespace is distinct from the capability-I/O namespace of
§4.1 -- an event's `anchors` is not a capability's `evidence_anchors`.

Three fields the spec marks MUST were declared but optional, and are now
required: `event.provenance`, `world_state.meta.version_id`, `meta.lineage`.
Per §11.4 that is breaking for producers which omitted them; no in-repo
fixture did.

Two further copies with nothing asserting they agree
